items.title: Non-Profit Community Support Services Program (CDBG-DR) Request for Applications: Mental Health 1 | Page 1.0 INTRODUCTION The City of St. Petersburg (the City) is issuing a competitive Request for Applications (RFA) to award U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) Community Development Block Grant–Disaster Recovery (CDBG‑DR) funds through the City's Non‑Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) Program. The NPCSS Program (also referred to as ‘the Program’) is built to strengthen the community by helping nonprofits offer the care and support people need after disaster, so residents can recover and prepare for the future. This RFA, the first in a series of funding opportunities under the NPCSS Program, is specifically focused on identifying subrecipients who will provide mental health and wraparound support services as described in this document. This is not a grantmaking opportunity where organizations apply to meet their individual needs; this is a solicitation where the City is procuring a specific set of services to meet the needs of city residents. EXPLANATION: Congress appropriated funds through the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) Community Development Block Grant - Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) Program in response to the 2023 Hurricane Idalia (DR-4734-FL) and the 2024 Hurricane Helene (DR-4828- FL). Assistance for these disasters was appropriated on December 21, 2024, by the Disaster Relief Supplemental Appropriations Act of 2025. The City of St. Petersburg (City) was allocated $159,884,000 per the Allocation Announcement Notice (90 FR 4759) published on January 16, 2025. On June 12, 2025, City Council approved the CDBG-DR Action Plan for the use of the federal grant funds (Resolution No. 2025-327) which allocated $6,000,000 to the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program. HUD approved the City’s Action Plan in August 2025 and executed the City’s Grant Agreement in February 2026. Through extensive public input and Unmet Needs and Mitigation Needs Assessments in the Action Plan, the City determined the need to create the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program to address the increased need for essential community services as a result of the qualifying disasters. When the area was first platted, the northern half was known as Coolidge Park. Eventually, neighbors came together to form an association known as Highland Grove. The neighborhood’s boundaries extended north to 40th Avenue North and west to 34th Street North. The Highland Grove Neighborhood Association was inactive for many years when a group of concerned neighbors came together in response to concerns about speeding on residential streets where children were playing. 8 That effort helped bring neighbors together and ultimately led to the re-establishment of an active neighborhood association in May 2018. As part of that process, residents voted to rename the neighborhood St. Pete Heights and establish the current, smaller boundaries. The new boundaries, seen in the map on the right, were intended to create a more cohesive and manageable neighborhood, with major, heavily trafficked roads also serving as natural transitions between neighborhoods. After re-establishing, St. Pete Heights residents sought to increase their visibility through the creation of a public-facing logo. Non-Profit Community Support Services Program (CDBG-DR) Request for Applications: Mental Health 4 | Page 2.0 TIE-BACK TO THE DISASTER All CDBG-DR funded public service projects/activities must address needs that directly or indirectly resulted from qualifying disasters and/or enhance the community's resilience in managing future disaster events. Following Hurricanes Idalia and Helene, nonprofit service providers across St. Petersburg reported a significant increase in demand for critical services, including mental health counseling, trauma recovery support, childcare, food security programs, and homelessness prevention initiatives. Damage to facilities, staffing shortages, and increased operational costs have strained the ability of these organizations to meet the needs of impacted and vulnerable populations. As summarized in the City’s Action Plan, “numerous [public] comments highlighted the value of mental health services, social service hubs, and nonprofit-led disaster recovery efforts, emphasizing the need for trauma-informed care and continuity of essential services during and after storms.” As one commenter stated: “The importance of addressing mental health needs is reinforc

Building mental health service delivery into emergency preparedness plans could help emergency management and public health programs address the mental health needs during short- and long-term disaster recovery, particularly among persons with limited financial resources. The St. Pete Heights Neighborhood is a 112-acre community located on the north-central edge of St. Petersburg, between 30th and 38th Avenues North, from I-275 to 28th Street North. The neighborhood’s name is derived from a love of the city and the area’s higher elevation. Its central location provides residents with access to major transportation corridors, employment centers, schools, parks, shopping, and downtown St. Petersburg. St. Pete Heights has a current population of 1,493 people. There was a 2.2% increase in population between 2010 and 2020 and a 5.9% increase in the number of households. The median household income in 2026 is $67,939 and is expected to increase to $87,353 by 2030. Neighborhood Context and History 7 The neighborhood is characterized primarily by single-family homes arranged on a traditional grid street network, with a mix of long-term residents and newer homeowners contributing to its evolving character. The commercial corridor along 28th Street North provides easy access to limited storefront businesses and services, while I-275 offers regional connectivity and accessibility. To receive these funds, the City is required to maintain an ongoing process for review of local policies, ordinances, resolutions, and plan provisions that increase the cost of housing construction, or of housing redevelopment, and to establish a tracking system to estimate the cumulative cost per housing unit from these actions for the period July 1– June 30 annually. The total estimated project cost is approximately $54.5 million, inclusive of construction, design and engineering, permitting, contingencies, and escalation. This estimate reﬂ ects the complexity of developing within an active infrastructure corridor, including utility coordination, stormwater management, structural constraints, and the integration of high-quality public realm amenities. Major cost drivers include exterior improvements (sitework, paving, landscape, and infrastructure), specialty features (programmed spaces, recreation elements, and structures), and supporting systems such as electrical, low-voltage, and signage. The cost strategy is structured to support a phased implementation approach, allowing the project to be delivered incrementally while aligning with funding opportunities, permitting timelines, and adjacent development. Formerly known as the Under-I Project, the park takes its name from Orlando’s tree canopy, with the stated goal of creating a vibrant, inclusive, and sustainable urban oasis beneath the interstate. The design, led by AECOM in partnership with the City of Orlando’s Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA), evolved through public workshops and an online survey and is organized around six guiding principles — Connection, Safety, Community, Greenery, Mobility, and Artistic Immersion. While the City may play a role in supporting capital improvements, grants, and other funding opportunities, the extent of that participation has not yet been established. A comprehensive and diversiﬁ ed ﬁ nancial strategy will therefore be needed to supplement earned revenue and support long-term operations and maintenance. ENTERPRISE MODEL VIABILITY AND REVENUE DIVERSITY At the St. Petersburg Pier, the enterprise facility generates signiﬁ cant annual revenue – approximately $1.5 million – through tenant leases and events. However, even with this substantial income, the Pier still relies on city subsidies for the remainder of its funding. Because of the unique constraints of Trails Crossing, an enterprise funding model – whereby the cultural linear park would operate like a self-sustaining private business – is currently not recommended. Given the scale of the project and anticipated operating needs, earned revenue alone is not expected to fully support capital implementation or ongoing operations. Instead, ﬁ nancial sustainability will depend on multiple funding sources working together—including public investment and grants, private and philanthropic support, sponsorships and major gifts, and earned revenue generated through programming and activation. The phased implementation strategy allows these funding sources to evolve over time. Early public investment and grant funding can help advance design, infrastructure, mobility, stormwater, and other capital improvements, while Friends of Trails Crossing (FTC) can build philanthropic, corporate, and fundraising capacity to support implementation, programming, and long-term operations. The Port handles a diverse range of heavy cargo, including petroleum, steel, and phosphate, while also in the process of expanding its cruise industry. According to a 2023 impact study, Port Tampa Bay contributes an estimated $34.6 billion to Florida’s economy and supports over 192,000 jobs statewide. This strategic location positions the region as a key trade and logistics hub. St. Petersburg itself operates a smaller port, Port of St. Petersburg, which primarily serves research vessels, private yachts, and marine science operations. The region is also well-connected by air, with Tampa International Airport, located 20 miles away, and the smaller St. Pete-Clearwater International Airport in nearby Clearwater. On July 14, 2026, the City Commission authorized a tentative millage rate of 6.0543 mills for FY 2026/2027. This rate is the same as the current adopted millage rate and is 5.84% more than the rolled-back rate of 5.7200 mills. The gross taxable value of property in the City, including new construction, is $12,165,367,159. On July 14, 2026, the City Commission authorized a tentative millage rate of .2865 mills for the annual debt service for FY 2026/2027. -ACCRUED INTEREST- Bond interest earned since the last interest payment, but not yet received. -ALPHA- A linear regressive constant that measures expected return independent of Beta. -ASSET ALLOCATION- The division of portfolio asset classes in order to achieve an expected investment objective. -BALANCED UNIVERSES - Public Funds, Endowments & Foundations, Corporate peer groups, and PSN peer groups. -BETA- A measure of portfolio sensitivity (volatility) in relation to the market, based upon past experience. -BOND DURATION- A measure of portfolio sensitivity to interest rate risk. -COMMINGLED FUND- An investment fund which is similar to a mutual fund in that investors are permitted to purchase and redeem units that represent ownership in a pool of securities. -CONVERTIBLE BONDS - Hybrid securities' that offer equity returns during rising equity markets and improved down-market protection. -CORE- An equal weighting in both growth and value stocks. -CORRELATION COEFFICIENT- A measure of how two assets move together. The measure is bounded by +1 and -1; +1 means that the two assets move together positively, while a measure of -1 means that the assets are perfectly negatively correlated.

Ms. Schmidt presented a Summary by Estimated Revenue and Type and requested Committee input on each of the revenue concepts. o Fire Assessment Fee - Committee consensus was in favor. o Parking Fee – Already in place. o Resiliency Fee ($7/ERU example) – Move forward and continue with more research. o Resident Services Fees - Committee consensus was in favor. o Parking-based Street Repair Assessment – Put a pause on it; not high priority. o CRA (TIF) – In process. o Enterprise Fund Fee Adjustments (utilities) - Committee consensus was in favor. o Road Tolls – Committee was not in favor. o Philanthropy / Foundation / Round- up / Naming – Committee consensus was positive except for billboards and advertising. o P3 – Low priority for now; more information needed. o Bonds / Capital tools – Four were in favor and one not . Staff will bring back a menu of bonding options, either project-specific or referendum before proceeding. o Grants – Pursuit of grants will continue. Getting strategic with the $4M undergrounding for Gulf Boulevard was emphasized. Chair Samorajczyk mentioned a $300K state grant for public docks funding. Staff will follow up.

Five Year Estimated Revenues, Expense and Reserves 2026-30 Ms. Schmidt explained the high-level five-year forecast, which assumed revenues grow about 3% annually and operating costs about 3.3%, with capital project estimates based on prior input. The city expects roughly $314 million in revenues versus about $29 million in operating expenses and $218 million in capital costs, resulting in a projected $157 million funding gap.

Member Garchow referenced a document that outlines a resident -led initiative addressing the City’s capital project backlog , comparing funded and unfunded projects, highlight ing the $235 million unfunded backlog, and propos ing investing an additional $3 million now to accelerate projects and reduce future costs. It also include d a “cost of waiting” chart, a proposed multi -year funding plan, and provisions for public progress tracking and periodic review. The document is part of the meeting record. Member Garchow also provided a comparison sheet of nearby community millage rates.

Ms. Schmidt asked the committee to consider infrastructure needs in the amount $218 million over the next five years (that predates the storms), Ad Valorem changes (House Bills that may eliminate at worst $4M in ad valorem income), c apital improvement needs for the next five years, and Enterprise Funds; they should operate like a business unit and sustaining revenues . Staff were seeking direction on where to focus their efforts.

Stormwater Utility System The stormwater system serves nearly 7,700 parcels. Due to minimal projected customer growth, baseline revenues are expected to stay flat at around $1.4 million annually through the forecast period. The FY 2026 budget relies on existing cash reserves to balance. While effective short-term, a long- term rate adjustment is required to avoid completely depleting these funds. Operating expenses have risen nearly 8% per year since 2021. The 2026 budget sits at $1.3 million and is projected to scale 3.8% annually to $1.6 million by 2031, driven by inflation, labor (4%), and health insurance (10%). The total stormwater capital improvement plan is $140.9 million (2026– 2031). $132.8 million will be covered externally via the Resiliency Fund. $8.1 million must be absorbed by the stormwater fund itself ($3.4 million via user rates and $4.8 million via new debt). The system is paying $256,000 annually on a 2015 revenue note, which will be paid off in 2030. To help fund the capital plan, a new State Revolving Fund (SRF) loan of roughly $353,000 annually will come online in 2030, seamlessly replacing the old debt.

Reserves will be strategically drawn down over the first three years to cushion the blow to consumers while still tracking toward the 90- day rate revenue reserve target by 2031. The recommended rate path was for 1 5% annual increases for 2027, 2028, and 2029, followed by smaller 6.5% increases in 2030 and 2031. This results in a cumulative rate adjustment of 72.5%. The initial 2027 rate places the city slightly above the regional surveyed average of $158.48 per year. Unlike the reclaimed water system, an alternative "smoothed" capital reduction plan cannot be calculated here. Because stormwater is billed as an assess ment, legally, the base fee can only fund city-wide improvements. The $132.8 million in resilience projects provide localized benefits to specific areas. If the city wishes to fund those projects outside the Resiliency Fund, it would legally have to establish distinct geographic zones and issue localized special assessments.

Director Schmidt provided a brief review of the proposed budget framework that was included in the meeting packet. She noted the City Manager's direction to keep full-time employee staffing flat, limit growth to modest CPI -based increases , and prioritize balancing operating and maintenance budgets before expanding spending. Key budget highlights included total projected revenue of approximately $88.2 million across all nine funds , estimated ending fund balance of approximately $26.5 million, and that t he apparent gap between revenues and fund balance is intentional, driven largely by one-time capital and resiliency projects that are expected to decline as projects are completed. Major budget assumptions were a 3.2% cost -of-living adjustment for employees, a 3.5% increase in employee health insurance , and that capit al project budgets will continue to change as projects are completed and funds are reappropriated. Director Schmidt provided a brief review of departmental highlights. She noted that Enterprise funds (wastewater, stormwater, reclaimed water, parking) are heavily influenced by capital project timing, ongoing rate studies, and transfers.

Revenues and Trends - Ms. Schmidt reviewed the City’s revenue trends, noting total FY 2027 sources of approximately $85.4 million, including $32.8 million in the General Fund. She highlighted major revenue sources such as property taxes, EMS reimbursements, parking, utility and franchise revenues, sales tax, enterprise fund rates, and outstanding FEMA reimbursements. She also discussed the potential impact of Amendment 3 on homestead tax revenue and emphasized the City’s effort to right-size enterprise fund fees so services are funded by users rather than property tax subsidies.

Wastewater Utility System The wastewater system serves roughly 3,600 bimonthly accounts. Under existing rates, 2026 revenues ($8.1 million) cover operating expenses but fail to fully cover existing debt or fund any capital investments, requiring grants and General Fund transfers to balance. Operating costs are growing at 4.6% annually (projected to hit $8.7 million by 2030). The single largest line item is wholesale wastewater treatment purchased from the City of St. Petersburg, which increases at 5% per year. The system has a $58.4 million capital improvement program. 60% ($34.7M) will be funded through new debt, adding $2.24 million in annual debt service starting in 2029. 21% ($13.3M) comes from grants. 18% ($10.4M) will be funded directly from user rates. The system is currently paying off existing debt (down to $1 million by 2030). Even with the new debt coming online in 2029, the proposed rate plan maintains a healthy debt service coverage ratio of 146– 151%, well above the 115% required legal minimum.

Capital Improvement Plan - Ms. Schmidt reviewed the Capital Improvement Plan, which includes $64.1 million across 78 projects, plus $15.9 million in enterprise fund projects for wastewater, stormwater, and reclaimed water. She noted that actual FY 2026 expenditures will be updated, with remaining funds reappropriated to FY 2027. Major projects include Fire Station 22, seawall and shoreline protection, hurricane repairs, roadway improvements, and the Gulf Boulevard undergrounding project, which is being evaluated with Duke Energy us ing the remaining $3.8 million grant.

Reclaimed Water System Mr. Ocasio reviewed key findings from the study. The system serves approximately 2,900 accounts. Rate revenue is projected to stay flat at around $1.1 million annually through FY 2030 due to minimal customer growth. Under existing rates, current revenues only cover standard operations and a portion of a $61,000 annual General Fund loan (payoff in 2039). Revenues are completely insufficient to fund capital investments. Rising Costs: Operating expenses have grown roughly 16% per year since 2021 and are projected to rise at 4.5% annually through FY 2030, driven by labor (4%), health insurance (10%), and county wholesale water rate increases (5%). The system requires $4.5 million between 2026 and 2031 for two major projects (lateral service pipe replacement and port installation), averaging $676,000 annually. The city bills based on parcel square footage rather than usage, making direct comparisons to other cities difficult. However, under the proposed changes, the rate would align closely with regional averages for heavy irrigation (25,000 gallons).
Fund totals $32.8 million in revenues and $32.6 million in expenditures, with expenses lower than FY 2026 mainly due to non-recurring transfers.

Fund Summaries - Ms. Schmidt reviewed the major enterprise and special revenue funds. The Building Fund is drawing down its fund balance for a new building and permitting software system. She noted that several funds, including the Resiliency, Multimodal, Capital Improvement, and Stormwater Funds, include projects that will be reappropriated into FY 2027 as work progresses. The Fleet Fund includes vehicle replacements, while the Wastewater and Reclaimed Water Funds reflect fee increases and necessary transfers to maintain adequate fund balances. Finally, the Parking Fund is operating as a separate fund for the first full year, with projected revenues of approximately $8.8 million to support street and beach maintenance, public safety, and other City projects.

To achieve the goal of eliminating reliance on General Fund subsidies and build a 90- day cash operating reserve by the end of the forecast period, t wo rate paths were presented . A) A 50% increase in 2027, followed by 8% annual increases through 2031 (cumulative increase of over 104%). The basic monthly service fee would jump immediately from $25.00 to $37.50 in 2027, reaching $51.02 by 2031. This would i mmediately cover the deficit previously funded by the General Fund and swiftly build up cash reserves. B) Use a phased approach to ease the initial 2027 rate spike, though it achieves the same ~104% cumulative increase by the end of the timeline. This requires cutting the near -term capital improvement plan by $700,000 on the front end, delaying some capital investments to a later date.

SUMMARY: The Board strongly advises the inquirer not to make this loan. He or she would become the lender to a City vendor whose work his or her own employees inspect. For 15 years, the inquirer could have a personal financial reason to favor that vendor. The Board considers the arrangement highly inappropriate, regardless of whether it violates the gift rule. The Board cannot give a favorable answer under Section 2-15 on the information provided. The final interest rate and other important loan terms are unknown. But those missing facts also do not establish a violation. To find a prohibited gift, the Board must identify a benefit the vendor gives the inquirer without receiving equal or greater value in return. Charging two percentage points above the bank’s interest rate does not, by itself, establish that the inquirer would receive a gift. This opinion supplements AO 2026-03, adopted September 15, 2026. Statement of Issue The City is requesting the Commission’s approval to apply to the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) for the Section 5311 Grant. This grant application covers Federal Fiscal Year 2027-2028. The grant will provide up to $360,000 of funding to allow StarMetro as the area’s Community Transportation Coordinator (CTC) to continue providing transportation services to residents in the non-urbanized areas of Leon County who have limited transportation choices. This grant specifically provides StarMetro the ability to fulfill trip request for individuals with limited mobility choices.

Approximately $17.8 million is anticipated to be available for EPA Region 4, which includes Florida. The maximum federal funding request is $4 million per application. Projects funded under this opportunity are expected to have a project period of two to four years.

The TDIA has identified the high cost of converting existing commercial space into retail and hospitality uses as one of the primary barriers to investment. While the existing Commercial Property Improvement Program (CPIP) provides valuable assistance, its dollar-for-dollar matching requirement and maximum grant amount of $200,000 have limited its effectiveness for projects involving significant tenant improvements and adaptive reuse needed for more active uses. Restaurants and other hospitality-oriented businesses often require substantial upfront investment for ventilation systems, fire suppression systems, grease traps, upgraded plumbing and electrical systems, ADA improvements, and expanded HVAC capacity. In most cases, these costs significantly exceed the value of improvements required for traditional office uses.

The Haven on Vine redevelopment project requires new firewater main infrastructure to provide fire protection services to the property and support the required fire sprinkler systems. Cathcart Construction Company – Florida, LLC provided preliminary budgetary pricing of $715,400 for the proposed installation. The final scope and pricing will be subject to completed engineering plans, permitting, and negotiations. A 15% contingency ($107,310) is requested to address unforeseen field conditions and necessary changes, resulting in a total not-to-exceed authorization of $822,710.

The City will fund the project through its State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) funds. The City will execute and record a mortgage lien and corresponding promissory note in the amount of $242,680.70 against the property to secure the financial assistance. The mortgage and promissory note will establish a 30-year affordability period commencing on the date the documents are executed. Consistent with the City's Local Housing Assistance Plan (LHAP) and applicable program guidelines, the assistance will be structured as a deferred, forgivable loan with a 30-year term. The loan will be forgiven at the conclusion of the affordability period, provided the homeowner has remained in compliance with all applicable loan terms and conditions and has not defaulted. Should the final project costs exceed the currently approved amount of $242,680.70, the mortgage and promissory note may be amended to reflect the additional costs, provided the total assistance does not exceed the $350,000 maximum assistance amount established in the City's LHAP.

The requirements of 40 U.S.C. 3704 are applicable to construction work and provide that no laborer or mechanic must be required to work in surroundings or under working conditions which are unsanitary, hazardous or dangerous. Staff recommends motion to approve: An Agreement with the Palm Beach Soil and Water Conservation District (District) in an amount not to exceed $79,000 to provide soil and water resource conservation services for Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 - 2027. The term of this Agreement is retroactive from October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027. SUMMARY: This Agreement provides funding for the District’s Resource Conservation Activities. The Agreement requires Palm Beach County (County) to provide $79,000 in funding to the District for payment of soil and water resource conservation services and health insurance benefits.
